explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires whenever the model sees a subword that begins a new word (i.e. a word‐initial BPE token).
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature picks out structured document‐metadata headers—those uppercase, number‐and‐abbreviation sequences you see in legal case citations (volumes, reporters, dockets, courts, dates), patent abstracts, image captions, WHOIS/server info blocks, article titles, etc.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires whenever the model is looking at the very first token of a new top-level chunk or line (e.g. XML/PHP prologues, section headers, code-block “var…”, list “dependencies:”, titles like “Quantification…”, etc.). In other words, it marks line-start or block-start tokens.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature detects blocks of legal/attribution boilerplate—copyright notices, data‐source disclaimers and “licensed under …” headers (e.g. Apache license text, “AS IS” clauses, source‐attribution notes).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on the single‐token “focus” of a query or definition—typically a lone identifier or placeholder (n, x, R, C, V, g, No., cover, etc.) that names the central variable, symbol, or key term the user is asking about.
explanations.negative_explanation:
small  
Represents the superlative adjective “smallest” (the “small” morpheme) used in numeric‐comparison questions to pick out minimal values.

(tab character)  
Flags literal tab characters that indent or separate columns/fields in structured text (e.g. database dumps, code listings).

(newline)  
Captures line‐break tokens used to delimit logical lines or blank‐line boundaries across code and prose.

Hispanic  
Marks the demographic label “Hispanic” when referring to an ethnic group in news or reports.

com  
Detects the “com” element in domain names, URLs or package/class identifiers (e.g. com.mysql, .com links).

Franc  
Highlights the “Franc” prefix in proper names (e.g. Francisco) in biographical or historical entries.

root  
Triggers on the “root” prefix in build-script identifiers (e.g. rootProject) denoting a project’s root configuration.

Young  
Fires on the “Young” prefix in stage or artist names (e.g. Young Buck) in music news contexts.

Flickr  
Ends up on the Flickr brand name in image‐gallery captions or photo credits.

marketing  
Catches folder or file-path segments labeled “marketing” (often in Media/Marketing Gallery contexts).

Internet  
Lights up on the word “Internet” in headlines, article titles, or tech/disaster reports.

Office  
Marks the term “Office” in commercial-real-estate or business listing descriptions.

Magazine  
Highlights the word “Magazine” when naming or discussing periodical publications.

Advertisements  
Detects the term “Advertisements” in marketing or editorial process descriptions.

VELCRO  
Fires on the VELCRO brand name in product listings for hook-and-loop fasteners.

Government  
Marks the word “Government” in official reports, policy analyses, or news commentary.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on the very start‐of‐file “prolog” or header markers—things like “<?xml…?>” or “<?php…?>” processing‐instructions, leading license‐comment blocks (`/**…*/`), BOM/unicode header characters, README titles (e.g. “android backup…”), etc.—i.e. the model’s signal for “you’re in the file’s metadata/header region.”
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on title‐ or header‐style spans—tokens forming the names of works or formal documents (comics, films, studies, series, legislation, etc.) often rendered in title case or all caps with numbers and punctuation.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on tokens that head entire documents or major sections—titles, headings or the very first word of an article/abstract/code block—marking “start‐of‐text” or “start‐of‐section” positions.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires strongest on the key content words—the topic-defining nouns and technical terms in a passage (e.g. “Arcana,” “Underlords,” “mRNA,” “innate,” “temples,” “operon,” etc.). It essentially marks the salient, domain-specific vocabulary that carries the main subject of the text.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects “file-level” or “section” markers in code—i.e. the syntactic tokens that open or label top-of-file metadata and structural boundaries (XML/HTML prologs and tags, DOCTYPE, import/using/namespace directives, comment-block and documentation annotations like //, /*…*/, @file, @param, license headers, etc.).
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is essentially a “block‐header” detector—it peaks on the first keyword or title token that opens a new section, file or module (e.g. “package”, “use”, “class…”, “source…”, article titles like “Development…”, “International…”, etc.). In other words, it flags section or file‐level headings/top‐level declarations.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires whenever the model sees a non‐initial “big” BPE piece—i.e. a long, multi‐character token that continues a word (or is a long repetition of the same character, as in a comment‐separator). In practice it lights up on the suffix/fragments of proper names and compounds (the “ather” in WEATHER, “alli” in palliative, “izu” in Meizu, “ña” in Braña, etc.) or on long runs of punctuation (////////////////////////////////).
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature detects markup-style section headings or titles (e.g. bolded or underlined labels like “**Summary**,” “**Introduction**,” “**Transcript**,” “===…===,” etc.) that signal the start of a new document section.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature lights up on the very top‐of‐document “preamble” markers—i.e. the tokens that start a file’s or document’s header or metadata block (case‐citation headings, license/comment banners, import/package declarations, XML/HTML comment tags, etc.).
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on tokens that are all-caps (often with digits or punctuation attached)—i.e. acronyms, initialisms or uppercase identifiers (CSS, IL-5, SCN5A, SAAF, RUN, PART/BTC, etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on high-visibility, initial-cap words that serve as headings, dateline markers or named-entity labels (proper nouns/acronyms) at the start of sections.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on BPE sub‐tokens that are the core “stem” of compound names or technical terms—especially those starting with a capital letter (e.g. “Dynamic,” “Tre,” “Swe,” “MEDIA,” “Elem,” “Bold,” etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on the very first subword of capitalized headings, titles or names in encyclopedic and scientific text—i.e. the uppercase prefix that kicks off a proper noun, section heading or technical term (e.g. “Wik-” in Wikipedia, “Phot-” in Photograph/Photonic, “Major-” in section titles, personal names like “Jonathan-,” honorifics “Mr.”/“MR,” brand prefixes “Len-,” technical-study prefixes “Magn-,” “Exper-,” “Quant-,” “Character-,” question-starters “Does-,” “Imp-,” etc.).
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on the “topic‐anchor” words that kick off new sections or events—key nouns or verbs (often proper names of places or major actions like “transfer,” “restore,” “travel,” etc.) that serve as discourse or section headers and signal a thematic shift.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is essentially a “prefix detector” for content-bearing tokens: it lights up on the first few letters (typically 3–4) of longer identifiers or proper nouns (often CamelCase/PascalCase words, acronyms or file‐path names), marking the boundary where a new semantic unit (the head of a compound token) begins.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on “label” tokens that name sections or fields in structured text—e.g. JSON/YAML keys (name, version, dependencies, author, cells, root, etc.), config‐file properties, form headings or field labels (CBSE, Q:, ALL:, FLAG S:, teamName, texturePack, symbol, created_at, etc.). It abstracts over any token that serves as a schema key or section header.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature lights up on tokens that kick off a new titled or formatted block—e.g. the bold markers, brackets or punctuation that introduce section headers, case‐citation headings, code/CSS block names, article titles, list bullets, etc. It’s essentially spotting “start‐of‐section” delimiters.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on “label” tokens that stand alone as prominent identifiers in titles, headings or code comments—i.e. single‐word proper names (Ross, John), acronyms or abbreviations (R, Ariz.), key title words (Of, Color), file/extensions or language markers (​.c, mysql), copyright “c,” etc.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on the definite article “The” when it heads a title‐ or abstract-style sentence that introduces a new topic or key concept.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on tokens that look like structured numeric or identifier metadata—years, section/case numbers, version or model codes, phone numbers, JSON keys, citation numbers, prices, etc.—regardless of domain (legal, academic, technical docs, product listings, code/config snippets). It abstracts the notion “this is a formal numeric ID/reference in a structured document.”

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on document‐header markers—things like news datelines (e.g. “WASHINGTON —”), photo‐credit or byline names (“Paul …/Corbis,” “Jonathan ‘Bomba’ Gonzalez”), and legal‐opinion citations (“23 N.Y.2d 253 (1968)”, “498 F.3d 645 (2007)”)—in other words, the tokens that introduce or label a text rather than its narrative content.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron lights up on high-content descriptive modifiers—think strong evaluative adjectives/adverbs (horrific, terrible, anticipated, potentially, complex) and their characteristic morphological markers (-ed/-ing/-ate suffixes or hyphens)—the kind of language you use to emphasize or specify the main idea in titles, headings, or emphatic statements.

explanations.positive_explanation:
Here’s a concise abstract concept for each feature based on its top‐activating contexts:

• Central  
  Detects the adjective “central,” especially in listings or ads emphasizing a downtown or core location (e.g. “central location,” hotel names containing “Central”).  

• b  
  Marks adult‐content listings (video codes, explicit sexual terms) typical of porn‐site metadata and descriptions.  

• Great  
  Flags strongly positive evaluative language in reviews or endorsements (“Great Cruise Line,” “felt secure,” “gave their best”).  

• 1  
  Identifies numbered list or section headings (“1.”) that introduce the first item or top‐level section in a document.  

• Republican  
  Picks up mentions of U.S. political party affiliation in campaign/election news (e.g. “Republican presidential nominee…”).  

• Jr  
  Highlights “Jr.” as a junior‐division or youth‐team designation in sports team names (e.g. “Springfield Jr. Blues”).  

• 17  
  Captures age‐denoting phrases (“17-year-old”) in human-interest or achievement stories.  

• John  
  Detects first-name personal references in profiles or memoir titles (e.g. “John Birt’s memoir”).  

• 12  
  Recognizes date-time stamps at the start of logs or updates (“12th Apr 2010, 15:39” etc.).  

• Robert  
  Flags celebrity-gossip headlines involving Robert Pattinson in entertainment news.  

• Getty  
  Spots “Getty Images” photo‐credit lines in news articles.  

• Richard  
  Identifies photographer credit lines from wire services (e.g. “Richard Drew/AP Photo”).  

• February  
  Marks event-announcement headings that begin with a spelled-out month and day (“February 6, 2007 …”).  

• AP  
  Flags Associated Press bylines or source tags at the top of news items (“AP source: …”).  

• WASHINGTON  
  Detects standard news datelines: uppercase city names (“WASHINGTON –”) indicating the article’s origination point.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is a “word-start” detector in the BPE/WordPiece sense—it fires on the first subword fragment of any multi-piece token (e.g. “cond” in “cond│ense,” “bott” in “bott│lenose,” “SPR” in “SPR│ings,” “Vend” in “Vend│ors,” etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is a structural‐cue detector that fires on the opening tokens of new sections, headings or titles—especially function words (articles, prepositions) and capitalized words that signal the start of a document block (e.g. court caption, blog post heading, “Introduction” sections, lead sentences).
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on the Swedish preposition “för” (meaning “for”), flagging that specific function‐word form in Swedish sentences.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on formal, uppercase multi‐word labels and titles in structured text—e.g. court or county names (“Court of Appeals of Texas,” “Travis County”), corporate or license headers (“Copyright (C) … Intel Corp.,” “Texas Instruments Inc.”), event or team headings (“Florida Gators,” “Toronto Festival of Beer”), XML/DOCTYPE tags, section titles, etc.—essentially marking institutional or document-metadata headings.
explanations.negative_explanation:
• Quaternion rotations: the feature fires on “quatern­ion” components when discussing 3D rotation operations.  
• Initialization markers: high on “init” in IL or code snippets, capturing field/method initializer directives.  
• Localhost addresses: activates on “localhost” in HTTP(S) connection contexts, denoting the local server host.  
• Polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs): peaks on “polymorpho­nuclear,” representing neutrophil white-cell biology.  
• AngularJS root scope: high on “$rootScope,” indicating the top-level scope in AngularJS dependency injection.  
• Ligands in binding assays: activates on “lig(and)” when describing molecular binding partners in fluorescence studies.  
• Substrates in biodegradation: fires on “substr(ate)” in co-digestion experiments, denoting feedstock molecules.  
• XML root element: high on “<root>,” representing the document’s root node in XML debug/info files.  
• Environment-variable commands: peaks on “env” (and “setenv”), capturing shell syntax for setting environment variables.  
• File-path handling in Node.js: fires on “path” in require/format calls, denoting file-system path resolution.  
• Directory name globals: activates on “dir(name),” capturing use of __dirname-style directory references.  
• Amino acids in dialysis studies: peaks on “amino acid,” denoting solute profiling in peritoneal dialysis research.  
• Session variables in SQL schemas: high on “vari­ables” within session_variables contexts, marking database session settings.  
• Cryptographic hashing: activates on “hash” in Bitcoin/verification code, representing cryptographic hash functions.  
• Database cursors in Java: fires on “cursor” in CursorAdapter or query contexts, denoting row-by-row result iteration.  
• Bioconjugates in biosensors: peaks on “jug(ate)” in immunosensor descriptions, representing molecular conjugation.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires whenever the text starts with a structured numeric identifier—most often the volume-number at the head of a legal reporter citation (e.g. “189 F. Supp. 2d 426 (2002)”), but more generally any leading number or year that introduces a formal reference (case citation, date range, flight no., list index, etc.).
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature flags passages formatted as code or formal notation—i.e. structured programming constructs (imports, function/variable declarations, shell‐make directives, braces, `$…$` math delimiters, etc.) and inline LaTeX/math expressions—across diverse technical Q&A contexts.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature marks tokens that occur as part of an explicit enumeration or list‐style structure (e.g. numbered filenames, comma- or newline-separated columns/imports/usings, JSON/Markdown arrays or tables) rather than running prose.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on opening or heading words – the initial, often capitalized token of a message or section (greetings like “Hello,” formal prefixes like “MR,” or title-style leads such as “THE,” “Recent,” “Long-term,” etc.) indicating the start of a new post, article heading, or section.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on tokens that introduce or refer to external dependencies or resources—e.g. import/extends/use/incorporate verbs, URLs and “://”, script‐src or namespace declarations, file‐path literals, etc.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on the very first, capitalized “topic” token that opens a news‐style headline or paragraph—e.g. WE, Students, CAN, Maps, Researchers, I, NASA, AMES, Obama, etc.—effectively marking the boundary or lead word of a new article or section.
